newsitem.title: UK: Mooted ACT cut may heighten UK gilt charm.
newsitem.headline: Mooted ACT cut may heighten UK gilt charm.

text.p: UK gilts are set to reap the rewards if Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown confirms media speculation by reducing or even abolishing Advance Corporation Tax (ACT) in his July 2 budget, analysts say.

The current system encourages the holding of equities rather than bonds by giving a tax credit of 20 percent on share dividend payments, so reducing ACT will tip the asset allocation balance back in favour of gilts.

In the case of tax exempt institutions such as pension funds, which own around half of the UK stock market according to the National Association of Pension Funds, the ACT credit actually means a cash refund.
"There's no doubt about it, cutting ACT would certainly give gilts an advantage on a relative basis," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders.
"I'm not sure whether anything is likely to happen to ACT in the short term term but its days are certainly numbered," he said.
The previous Conservative administration, ousted May 1, set a precedent by reducing ACT to 20 percent, from 33 percent during its 18-year rule.
In 1993, then Chancellor of the Exchequer Norman Lamont trimmed the rate to its current level of 20 percent from 25 percent, increasing government revenue by 1.0 billion stg.
The equity market is now nervous that current Chancellor, Brown, will also try to boost revenue by reducing ACT, perhaps to 15 percent or even go further and scrap it.

IFS senior research economist Lucy Chennells estimates that rises in dividend payments mean ACT now garners around 12.0 billion stg a year compared with only around 8.0 billion at the time of the Lamont reduction. Cutting it to 15 percent could raise an additional 1.5 billion, she said.

ACT is an unusual tax in that reducing it actually increases government revenue. Companies pay ACT at 20 percent to cover their dividend payments to shareholders and can then offset the amount paid against their overall tax bill.

Cutting the rate paid by companies means they pay a smaller amount of ACT but there is then a corresponding reduction in the amount to offset against their overall tax bill. There is therefore no impact on the total amount of tax they pay.
The tax credit is the crucial area which allows higher revenue.
Firstly, a lower ACT rate saves the Treasury money because it has to refund less to tax exempt shareholders.

Secondly, holders of shares who are liable to the higher rate of income tax -- currently 40 percent -- must pay the difference between the ACT tax credit and the top rate of tax. So their tax bills will rise.
There are two major considerations for the British equity market, according to BZW.
The first is the valuation concern from the implied reduction in the gross dividend yield on equities caused by the cut in the tax credit.
The second is the impact on equities relative to gilts.

"Pension funds -- non-tax paying institutions -- already have a preference for gilts," said BZW strategist Steve Wright. "We've seen pension funds switch away from equities as it is and any move to cut ACT could exacerbate this," he said.
Pension funds sold 8.6 billion stg of equities last year, with 3.3 billion going into gilts and 5.8 billion going into cash, he said.
"Much of this was down to passive selling because of bid activity but it shows that pension funds don't have much of an appetite for equities. They would much rather have gilts."
The gilt/equity dividend yield ratio, which is used to measure the relative performance of the two markets, is currently low at around 2.06.
This is a level which would normally be regarded as a buy signal for equities, said Charterhouse Tilney group chief economist Richard Jeffrey.

But the recent changes to the framework of British monetary policy have increased confidence in the country's chances of holding down inflation and thus the risk premium demanded by investors for holding gilts has fallen.
Moreover the same changes -- empowering the Bank of England to decide interest rates -- may also have also damaged the growth prospects of the economy thus depressing the outlook for company profits.
Together these factors mean that the dividend yield ratio may have some way to fall before equities rather than gilts look attractive.

"The shift in policy has, if anything, lowered the long term growth potential of the economy. That's also bad for equities," said Jeffrey. "My feeling is the yield ratio ought to be lower than it actually is. The yield on equities should be higher."
Reducing ACT would be yet another factor that would allow a lower dividend yield ratio before gilts look overvalued compared with shares.
"It obviously makes gilts and high yielding convertibles more attractive. Pension funds will be looking for income and this adds to the trend towards fixed income," Jeffrey said.

BZW's Wright agreed that the yield ratio was unlikely to provide support for the equity market and said it could fall to around 1.79, the low seen in 1992 when Britain fled the EU's exchange rate mechanism, if ACT is reduced.

Combined with moves towards convergence in European bond markets on expectations of European monetary union, the threat to ACT is another factor improving the allure of gilts. "Pension funds are going to be even more interested in shifting assets from equities into gilts," Wright said.

The other key measure of relative value -- the yield gap between the FT-All share index and that of index-linked gilts is already flagging equities as over-valued compared with gilts, with a negative yield gap of around 20 basis points.
Cutting ACT could see the yield gap move up to around 25 basis points, back in positive territory whilst abolishing it altogether could push it right up to 50, Wright said.
Aside from the possibility of raising extra revenue, there are a number of other factors which may tempt the new government to trim or even abolish ACT.
"If they are planning to introduce a lower income tax rate of 10 percent, then it would make sense to reduce ACT to a similar level," SBC Warburg economist Darren Winder said.
The current 20 percent ACT rate is the same as the current bottom income tax rate. Labour has pledged to try to reduce the starting rate of tax, in a bid to help the lower paid.

Moreover, there is some argument that the current system encourages companies to distribute a high proportion of their profits to shareholders -- many of whom are tax exempt pension funds -- rather than retaining them for investment.

Whilst Labour was in opposition, it said repeatedly that it wanted to end "short-termism" in industry and analysts say this could be a sign ACT is on their hit list but it should also imply bigger tax incentives for investment, which would eat up any extra revenue.

But the case for getting rid of ACT is not clear cut, HSBC James Capel analysts deny ACT means high dividend payments are crowding out other investment decisions and argues that trying to use ACT abolition as a fund raiser is an non-starter.
Abandoning ACT would lead to a revaluation of pension funds because of the 20 percent reduction in income.
"Estimates made in 1993 suggested that a large number of pension funds would then become underfunded, requiring additional contributions," Capel analysts said in their "ACT No Free Lunch" document.
"These would be made from pre-tax profit, leading to a revenue shortfall almost equivalent to the saved ACT."

Analysts warn that the issue of ACT is too complex for rushed decisions and moreover, during the last few years of its 18 years in opposition, Labour was assiduous in trying to shake off its anti-business image. Smacking pension funds within a couple of months of taking office could undo much of its success in this direction.

"It goes against the spirit of what they've been trying to do. They've spent a long time building up a relationship with the City, to come out and abolish ACT quickly could throw it all away," said Schroders Philpotts.
